steps.action:
The last ferry of the season left the island on a gray October afternoon, its wake a white scar across the slate water. Silas Rourke stood on the pier and watched it go, one hand resting on the brass rail of his lantern, the other buried deep in the pocket of his wool coat. The boat grew smaller until it passed behind the headland and was gone, leaving only a faint shudder of waves against the rock.

“Just you and me now,” he said to the sea, though he meant the lighthouse that loomed behind him.

Gull Point Light had stood on the island for eighty-seven years. Its stone tower rose from the spine of rock like a bone, the white paint peeling in long curls, the black lantern room crowned with a weather vane that forever pointed east. Generations of keepers had lived here, lighting the great Fresnel lens each dusk, trimming the wick, polishing the glass, logging the ships. In recent years, the shipping lanes had shifted and the light had been automated, but the Maritime Authority still kept a caretaker on-site—someone to maintain the machinery, clear the lenses, record the weather, and, unofficially, to make sure the place didn’t simply give up and crumble into the sea.

Silas had taken the job five years ago, not because he loved the sea particularly, but because he had once loved the noise of a city too much. When the sounds of traffic and voices and sirens had started to echo in his skull long after they’d ceased, when sleep came only with the help of pills and finally not at all, he’d found an advertisement in the classifieds: CARETAKER NEEDED, REMOTE STATION, LONG PERIODS OF ISOLATION. EXPERIENCE PREFERRED, NOT REQUIRED.

He had looked up from the newspaper at his one-room apartment, at the murky window that admitted more neon than sun, and thought: Yes. That.

So he’d come to the island with too many books and too few expectations, and the lighthouse had taken him in the way only buildings on the edge of the world can—indifferently at first, then with a fierce, weather-beaten intimacy.

Now, with the ferry gone, winter began.

Silas climbed the path from the pier to the tower, his boots crunching on frost-stiffened grass. The wind dragged at his coat, smelling of iron and salt. He passed the oil house, squat and dark, and the old fog bell that no longer rang, its tongue stilled and rust-red. The keeper’s cottage huddled beside the tower, white clapboard with green shutters, smoke already rising from its chimney. He had banked the fire that morning, knowing that once the ferry left, there would be no more easy visits to the mainland for supplies. Whatever he had now would have to last until spring.

Inside the tower, the air changed: stone-cool, smelling faintly of kerosene and metal polish. He began the climb up the spiral stairs, hand sliding along the smooth iron rail where the touch of a hundred hands had worn the paint thin. The narrow windows offered slices of sky, each one a slightly different shade of dusk. At the top, he unlocked the door to the lantern room and stepped into a circle of glass and wind.

The lens dominated the space, a tall glass beehive of prisms and curves, still miraculous to him after all this time. When he’d first arrived, a technician from the Authority had taken him through the maintenance procedures, referring to the lens simply as “the apparatus.” Silas had nodded, memorizing the steps, but in private he had given it a name: Lucia, for light. It made the routines feel less like chores and more like tending an animal that happened to be made of glass and light.

He circled the lens slowly, checking for smudges or chips. The autopilot system hummed quietly inside its metal casing. A green light glowed steady. All as it should be.

“Evening, Lucia,” he said. “How’s the view?”

The view was, as always, enormous. The horizon folded over itself in layers of slate and pewter. Far out, the faint shadow of another island lay low in the water like a sleeping animal. Above, the sky was a pale, exhausted blue bruised with darker clouds. The first star showed, then another.

He cleaned a faint salt smear from the outer pane with a chamois cloth, then checked the emergency crates stacked against the far wall—flares, spare bulbs, a hand-crank radio, a sealed tin of biscuits that might have been older than he was. Satisfied, he flipped open the logbook on the narrow desk by the door and wrote the date, the time, the weather, the sea state. His handwriting had grown neat and small over the years, compressed by the margins of the page as if he could fit his whole life between the lines.

October 28, 18:07. Overcast. Wind NE, 15–20 knots. Swell 1–2 m. Visibility 5 nm. Ferry departed. Winter watch commences.

There was comfort in the formality. The world might do as it pleased, but in this circle of glass and stone, there was an order he could maintain.

By the time he finished the entry, the automation had done its work. The bulb glowed, and Lucia’s prisms caught the light, shaping it, condensing it, and sending it out across the darkening sea in long, sweeping beams. Silas leaned his forehead briefly against the cool glass. Outside, the wind rose, tugging at the tower, and somewhere down below a wave exploded against the rocks with a sound like distant artillery.

That night the storm came in earnest, a slow-building fury that began with rattling shutters and ended in a sustained howl around the tower. Rain hammered the glass. The sea hurled itself at the island, foam boiling white in the brief moments when the sweeping lamp illuminated it.

Silas lay in his narrow brass bed in the keeper’s cottage, the covers pulled to his chin, listening to the house creak and sigh. He had once feared these gales, imagining the tower toppling, the glass shattering, the sea pouring in. In his second winter on the island, an equinoctial storm stronger than this had raged for three days straight. At the height of it, he had climbed to the lantern room because the idea of not being there—of Lucia’s light going out while he lay safe in his bed—felt worse than any danger. The wind had slammed him against the railing, the glass had flexed like a living thing, but the tower had held. It always did.

“Old bones,” he murmured now into the dark. “You know these storms better than I do.”

Outside, the foghorn moaned, a long, low note on a timer that seemed as old as the sea. Silas listened, counting the seconds between blasts. Eighteen. Again. Eighteen. The pattern soothed him, a metronome for the ocean’s restlessness.

Sleep came in fits, interrupted by particularly savage gusts or by the sharp crack of something—driftwood, he hoped—striking the shore. It was sometime in the small hours when a different sound woke him, not of wind or water, but of metal knocking against metal: a faint, irregular clanging, out of time with the foghorn.

He lay still, listening. There it was again: a hollow bang, pause, bang-bang, as if something were striking the pier ladder.

He swung his legs out of bed, the floorboards cold under his feet, and dressed quickly. Oilskin jacket, wool cap, boots. He took the big hand lamp from its hook by the door and tested it once, the beam cutting a clean tunnel through the cottage’s dim interior.

Outside, the wind slapped him full in the face, stealing his breath. The rain had eased to a fine mist, but the waves were still high, hurling themselves at the rock in sheets of white spray. Silas bent into the wind, lamp clutched to his chest, and made his way down the path toward the pier, his boots slipping on slick stone.

Near the edge, the clanging grew louder, more insistent. He shone the lamp ahead and saw the cause: a small aluminum skiff, its bow line snapped, slamming repeatedly against the ladder. One oar was still lashed inside; the other floated nearby, riding the waves like a black tongue. The skiff’s stern rose and fell, threatening to capsize with each surge.

Silas’s guts tightened. No one should be out in such seas, not in a boat this size. Yet here it was.

He swept the lamp’s beam out across the churning water. “Hello!” he shouted into the wind. “Ahoy! Anyone out there?”

The sea roared in reply, indifferent.

He tried again, voice raw. “Is anyone there?”

The foghorn moaned, then the skiff slammed into the ladder with a jolt that sent vibrations up through the rock into his soles. He couldn’t see anyone in the boat, but the night was a theater of illusions: whitecaps that looked like hands, shadowed swells that became hulking shapes.

A responsible man, he told himself, would record the incident in the log and call the mainland on the radio. He would not, under any circumstances, go climbing down a slippery metal ladder into a storm with only a lamp and an old length of rope for comfort. That would be reckless, possibly suicidal, definitely against protocol.

He tied the end of the rope around the pier’s heavy iron cleat, looped the other end twice around his own waist, and began down the ladder.

The first wave hit him halfway down, spraying up his legs and soaking him to the knees. Cold stabbed through the wool of his socks. He gritted his teeth and descended another rung, the ladder vibrating with each strike of the skiff. When he reached the bottom step, the boat swung toward him like a pendulum, its metal lip level with his chest.

He timed it: swing away, swing back—and then he stepped off the ladder and into the boat, catching the gunwale with one hand, lamp clutched high in the other.

The skiff bucked under his weight. For a moment he was sure they would both go over, but then the boat settled, rising and falling with the swell. Up close he could see that the bow line had frayed in the middle, not cut; the sea had done this.

The skiff was empty.

No life jacket, no bag, no thermos, no sign anyone had ever sat on the bench seats at all, save for a faint scuff where boots might have rubbed. He turned in a full circle, lamp sweeping the water. Nothing. Only the endless black backs of waves rolling and rolling toward shore.

“Damn,” he whispered, not sure if it was a curse or a prayer.

He secured the skiff to the ladder with what remained of the bow line, then climbed back up, his clothes heavy with seawater. At the top, he hauled on the rope wrapped around his waist, pulling the boat in until it snugged against the pier. There was nothing more to be done tonight. If someone had been in that boat, the sea had already decided their fate.

Back in the cottage, he stripped, hanging his wet clothes over the stove, and wrapped himself in a blanket. He made tea with shaking hands, the kettle’s thin whistle almost lost in the groan of the storm. After, he climbed to the lantern room, because he could not bear the thought of lying in bed while that little skiff knocked and knocked in his mind.

Lucia’s light swept the sea with tireless regularity. The automation box hummed, perfectly indifferent to skiffs and storms and men. Silas pressed both palms to the glass, feeling it tremble faintly with the wind. Below, the island was a hunched black shape ringed with white rage. No boat could have survived long out there, not without a miracle.

He stayed until the first pallor of dawn bled into the east, then went down and radioed the mainland station.

“Harbor Control, this is Gull Point Light,” he said when the crackling resolved into a human voice. “Unmanned skiff found at base of pier, storm last night. No persons observed. Requesting record and any missing vessel reports.”

The man on the other end sounded half-asleep. “Copy that, Gull Point. We’ll log it and call around. Any markings on the boat?”

Silas gave the hull number, the make, the color. There was a pause long enough that he could hear, faintly, a radio playing in the background on the mainland side.

“Well, that’s odd,” the harbormaster said finally. “That skiff belongs to the old Jennings place—little cottage up the estuary. Far as I know, no one’s used it in years. Folks inherited it moved away.”

Silas frowned. “So…no one would have taken it out in this weather.”

“Not likely. Could’ve worked its way loose from a rotten dock. Storm like that, things go wandering. We’ll send someone to check the cottage when the sea calms. In the meantime, just secure the boat, will you?”

“Already done,” Silas said, but his frown remained after he signed off.

He went down to the pier again after breakfast. In the thin, washed-out daylight, the skiff looked unremarkable, a battered little boat with peeling blue paint and a sticker on the stern that read “Jennings 1998.” It rocked gently in the now-tamer swell, bumping the ladder with a soft, irregular tap.

He stepped into it again, more carefully this time, and searched beneath the seats. A spider scuttled away from the sudden light. Long, dried lines of salt marked where water had once lapped as high as the bench. Nothing else. No clothing, no stray glove, no note.

On impulse, he sat. The boat dipped, then steadied. From here the lighthouse loomed above him, a pale pillar against the low sky. Lucia’s lamp was off for the day, but he could feel its presence—an eye shut, but not asleep.

The winter passed slowly after that, each day like the one before, and yet the found skiff made a new current run beneath the sameness. When the gales blew, he heard its ghostly knocking in his dreams. On calm days, he would row it in slow loops around the island, partly to give his land-stiff muscles something to do, partly to reassure himself that it was, in fact, just a boat.

Sometimes, on those quiet circuits, he spoke aloud.

“Why’d you come here?” he’d ask the empty stern. “All the sea to choose from, and you end up on my ladder.”

The skiff never answered, of course. But over time, Silas found his questions changing.

“What would’ve happened if I hadn’t come?” he mused one milky afternoon, oars creaking, the island’s cliffs reflected in the water like a face in broken glass. “If there had been someone. If they’d called, and there’d been no light, no horn, no fool on a ladder with a rope around his waist.”

He had taken this job to escape noise, to flee the press of other people’s lives against his own. Out here, the days were his to arrange as he pleased. And yet, the routine of tending the light was, at its core, an act of hospitality toward strangers he would never meet. It was a promise extended across the dark water: I will be here. I will keep the flame.

The idea settled around him slowly, like a cloak.

One night near the end of January, a call came through on the radio. The mainland voice was sharper this time, edged with weather and worry.

“Gull Point, this is Harbor Control. We’ve got a fishing boat overdue, the Doreen May. Last seen heading home ahead of this front. Radar puts her somewhere near your position. Visibility’s dropping. Keep an eye out, will you?”

Silas glanced instinctively toward the window, though he already knew what he’d see: fog thick as unspun wool, pressing close to the glass, swallowing the world beyond the first ring of rocks.

“Copy that,” he said. “Light’s operational. Foghorn sounding. I’ll report any contact.”

He climbed the tower and checked everything twice—bulb, lens, rotation. The automation had never failed him, but tonight he watched Lucia’s beam sweep the fog again and again, the light carving out a moving tunnel that vanished thirty meters from the glass. The foghorn bellowed in its eighteen-second rhythm, and between each note he listened, heart drumming a staccato under the slow, patient bass.

The hours stretched. He drank coffee that went lukewarm in its mug. He paced the narrow circle of the lantern room until he knew every chip in the paint, every bolt head by heart. Down below, the island had shrunk to a small, certain geometry—cottage, path, pier—floating in a sea of featureless gray.

It was just past midnight when he heard it: a faint, distant horn, higher-pitched than his own fog signal, stuttering in the spaces between Lucia’s rotations. He froze, straining to separate the sounds.

There—a short, panicked blast, then another. A boat, close enough to hear him, lost in the blind white world.

He grabbed the handheld radio. “Doreen May, this is Gull Point Light. Can you hear me?”

Only static answered. He tried again, voice louder, but if they replied, their words dissolved into crackle and hiss.

He set the radio down and pressed his hands to the glass, forehead tight against the cold. “Come on,” he whispered. “See us. Just see us.”

Outside, the fog swallowed his voice. Only the light went on, and on, its invisible beam a metronome for his fear.

He imagined the boat’s crew—faces he’d never seen, names he would only learn later if things went badly—huddled on a bucking deck, peering into a wall of white, listening for a horn. He imagined them straining for any sign that the world still had edges, that land existed somewhere beyond this sameness.

His whole life had, in some way, been a pendulum between wanting to be seen and wanting to vanish. Out here, he had chosen the latter, letting the sea erase his old self with its relentless passing days. Now he found himself on the other side of that equation, the unseen man whose single job was to make sure others did not disappear.

He checked the backup bulbs. He checked the generator. He adjusted the foghorn timing by a fraction, not because it needed it, but because the act of doing something, anything, made breathing easier.

Hours later, just before dawn, the fog thinned abruptly, going from a suffocating wall to a thin, torn curtain. In that lifted veil, he saw her: a fifty-foot trawler, green hull, white cabin, riding low in the swell, maybe half a mile off. Her bow was pointed not toward the harbor channel but toward the reef that jutted invisible beneath the surface—jagged teeth that had chewed up more than one hull when the light was new and her keepers still burned whale oil.

Silas gripped the brass railing hard
